findings.problem: BudgetWorkflow uses String for status and separate bool flags (is_validated, is_sent) instead of typed enums or typestates. The compiler cannot prevent illegal state combinations such as status=\"sent\" with is_validated=false, or is_sent=true with status=\"draft\".
findings.failure_mode: Any caller can construct BudgetWorkflow with inconsistent lifecycle fields, creating unobservable invalid states that silently corrupt workflow semantics.
findings.fix: Replace status: String with a domain enum (e.g., BudgetStatus { Draft, Validated, Sent, Rejected }) and replace is_validated/is_sent bools with a typestate on BudgetWorkflow itself (e.g., BudgetWorkflow<S: WorkflowState>). Eliminate redundant flags; derive derived state from the enum.

findings.problem: id is a raw String instead of a typed newtype BudgetId. The domain identity has rules but they are not enforced by the type system.
findings.failure_mode: Callers can pass any string as an id, including empty, malformed, or externally injected values. No domain-level invariants on identifiers are enforced at the type level.
findings.fix: Introduce a newtype struct BudgetId(String) with a fallible constructor that validates domain invariants. Use BudgetId everywhere the budget identifier is needed.

findings.problem: mark_sent has no precondition enforcement. It marks a budget as sent without requiring the workflow to be in a validated state. The bool is_validated field is ignored entirely.
findings.failure_mode: A budget can be marked as sent without ever being validated, violating the workflow invariant that sent budgets must first be validated. This is a business logic bypass that the type system should prevent.
findings.fix: Use typestates so mark_sent is only callable on a validated typestate. For example: fn mark_sent<S: ValidatedState>(workflow: BudgetWorkflow<Validated>) -> BudgetWorkflow<Sent>. Remove the is_validated bool and make validation a compile-time state transition.

findings.problem: item.status = \"sent\".to_string() allocates a new String each time mark_sent is called. Since status should be an enum, this allocation is unnecessary.
findings.failure_mode: Unnecessary heap allocation on every state transition. Not a correctness issue but a performance anti-pattern in the core.
findings.fix: Replace String status with a stateless enum variant. Enum variants are zero-cost copies with no allocation.

findings.problem: All fields of BudgetWorkflow are pub, allowing external callers to mutate fields directly and bypass all invariants.
findings.failure_mode: External code can set item.is_sent = false after mark_sent was called, or set item.status = \"sent\" while item.is_validated remains false, creating inconsistent state without going through any domain method.
findings.fix: Make all fields private. Provide a fallible constructor (e.g., BudgetWorkflow::new(id, initial_status)) and explicit transition methods that enforce invariants. Use typestates for compile-time guarantees.

findings.problem: is_validated (bool) and is_sent (bool) are redundant with the status field. This three-field representation (status string + two bools) can easily drift into inconsistent states.
findings.failure_mode: Drift: callers can set status=\"validated\" but leave is_sent=true from a prior operation, or set is_validated=true but status=\"draft\".
findings.fix: Collapse all three fields into a single BudgetStatus enum. Derive is_validated and is_sent as queries (e.g., .is_validated() -> bool) from the enum, never stored separately.

missing_evidence: no benchmark exists for mark_sent allocation behavior
no profiler data for BudgetWorkflow lifetime or hot paths
no allocation audit (no #[global_allocator] test or allocation-tracking harness)
no command-line entry point or CLI binary defined in Cargo.toml
residual_risk: Static review only; no commands run. The crate's core domain model is fundamentally underspecified: primitive types for state, redundant fields, and no typestate enforcement create unpreventable illegal states. The fix is architectural (enum/typestate refactor) rather than incremental. No behavior tests exist to validate the intended workflow invariants.
